title: Meteorite Dust Preserved a Magnetic Record from the Birth of the Sun
mediaSource: primitive meteorite magnetic field early solar system Antarctica CAI grains laboratory

scenes.title: Meteorite dust preserved the solar system's first magnetism
scenes.narration: Tiny grains inside a primitive Antarctic meteorite preserved traces of a magnetic field from the very beginning of the solar system.

scenes.title: The material formed in the first 200,000 years
scenes.narration: The team studied calcium-aluminum-rich inclusions, some of the oldest known solids, formed within roughly the first two hundred thousand years of solar system history.

scenes.title: Tiny minerals remembered an ancient field
scenes.narration: Magnetic minerals inside the grains locked in information about the magnetic field around them and preserved that record for billions of years.

scenes.title: The field may have been stronger than Earth's
scenes.narration: Measurements suggest the early solar system's magnetic field may have been roughly three to twelve times stronger than Earth's magnetic field today.

scenes.title: Gravity may not have worked alone
scenes.narration: Scientists have long emphasized gravity in forming the Sun. The new evidence suggests magnetism also helped move gas and dust through the young solar nebula.
keywords: solar nebula gas dust magnetic field

scenes.title: A meteorite fragment remembers the Sun's birth
scenes.narration: A tiny rock that eventually fell to Earth may still carry a record from 4.6 billion years ago. The Sun's birth may have been shaped by both gravity and magnetism.
